The other extreme is represented by findings such as the “flag study” of Carter et al. (2011). As Ferguson et al. (2014) argued, this is basically a historical effect, namely that at a certain time in American history, American citizens became more conservative, when primed with the American flag. But many findings in the social psychological literature may reflect general laws, even though the experimental manipulations used are susceptible to historical change. Those are the studies, where conceptual instead of exact replication is appropriate. A classic example is the study by Aronson andMills (1959) on the effects of severity of initiation on liking for a group (see Footnote 2). Although their severity manipulationwould be unlikely to be effective these days, this would not invalidate their theoretical hypothesis. If their manipulation was replaced by some other task that was considered effortful or embarrassing by present day students, their finding might be replicated. Another example would be the manipulation of argument quality in tests of dual process models of persuasion,where argument strength is typically defined empirically for each specific subject population (e.g., Petty & Cacioppo, 1986). Historical change can also affect the dependent measure, even in experiments that test basic psychological processes. To give one example, Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988) tested the hypothesis that people's facial activity influences their affective responses. They had their student participants hold a pen in their mouth in ways that either inhibited or facilitated muscles typically associated with smiling. Their dependent measure consisted of ratings of the funniness of a set of cartoons that had been rated asmoderately funny in a pretest. In support of the facial feedback hypothesis, Strack et al. (1988) found that the cartoons were rated least funny, when the muscle activity associated with smiling was inhibited.
